newsitem.title: USA: Pork prices soar on Taiwan news, grains also jump.
newsitem.headline: Pork prices soar on Taiwan news, grains also jump.

text.p: Pork prices soared on Thursday after Taiwan said it was halting pork exports due to a disease outbreak, feeding speculation that the United States would soon be tapped by Japan and other nations for more pork.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly futures for May delivery closed up the daily trading limit of 3 cents a pound at 76.30 cents and June hogs up the 2.00 cents a pound daily limit at 78.150 cents.
The Taiwan Council of Agriculture said it was banning all exports of fresh and frozen pork temporarily due to an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease among pigs in nine counties and 20 breeding farms.
Taiwan said curbing the highly contagious disease would be hampered by shortages of vaccines in Taiwan.
Japan has been importing about 16,000 metric tons of pork from Taiwan each month -- demand that could be filled by pork producers in the United States, Canada and Europe.
"This is an important event, but we don't know the significance until we know all the facts," said Al Tank, chief executive officer of the National Pork Producers Council.
"If true, it would be a very significant development that clearly the United States, Denmark and Canada would be the greatest beneficiaries of," Tank said.

Last year U.S. pork exports to Japan totalled 183,193 tons, up 36 percent from shipments in 1995. The sales rose despite a special tariff Japan slapped on the flood of pork imports in July 1996. It is due to be lifted on July 1.
Traders said other buyers of Taiwanese pork, such as South Korea, could also be expected to turn to other suppliers until Taiwan can certify its pork is disease-free.

Cattle prices shrugged off the gains in pork values, with June live cattle closing down 1.225 cents a pound at 63.475 cents. Traders cited a weak cash cattle market and higher corn prices as reasons for the selling.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain prices were led higher by soybeans as professional fund investors returned to the market in force after news of strong weekly exports.
May soybeans rose 13 cents a bushel to close at $8.52 and May corn closed up 2 cents a bushel at $3.04-1/2.

Pit traders said commodity funds bought up to 30 million bushels of soybeans after the Agriculture Department said export sales in the week ending March 13 were 428,400 tons, compared to expectations for 300,000 to 400,000 tons.
The strong sales calmed fears that cheaper supplies now being harvested in Brazil and Argentina would cut exports.
"Everybody says it's going to slow down, but so far it's not slowing down. Exports were good for everything," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.
Demand for soybeans by domestic processors also remained red-hot, with the U.S. Census Bureau reporting February's "crush" at 125.152 million bushels, a record for the month.
"The February crush number was strong," said Allen Dever, a soybean market analyst with Doane Agriculture Services.
"Clearly we're running at a pace we cannot sustain or we'll run out of soybeans," Dever said.
Corn prices were supported by news that the crop in South Africa, a competing exporter, was expected at 7.564 million tons, down sharply from last year's 9.484 million tons.
Weekly export sales were also a strong 867,700 tons.

May wheat futures closed 6-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $3.97-1/2 as traders focused on worries about how possible flooding in Minnesota and the Dakotas could delay planting and hurt yields in this year's spring wheat crop.
"We still have the threat of flooding this spring," said analyst Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, refined oil product prices closed lower as worries about supply eased.
April unleaded gasoline closed 0.38 cent a gallon lower at 67.58 cents and April heating oil down 0.35 cent at 55.94 cents a gallon.
At least one major refiner, Exxon Corp., said operations at its facility at Baton Rouge were running "normally" after a barge accident restricted shipping along the Mississippi River.
April crude oil closed 28 cents a barrel higher at $22.32 as traders said oil companies shifted positions.
"The story was refiners rolling their short positions into May and out of April," said Dimon Oil Co. vice president Herb Harris.
